notes.title: Start here: one reference app, three chapters on its architecture
notes.body:
Bulletproof React is a reference architecture: one discussion-board app built three times (`apps/react-vite`, `apps/nextjs-app`, `apps/nextjs-pages`) to show how a React codebase can stay maintainable as it grows. This quest uses the `react-vite` app and three chapters of `bulletproof-react/fable-docs/`:

1. `02-project-structure.md`: how folders are organised and which imports are allowed.
2. `05-api-layer.md`: the one API client and the per-endpoint file pattern.
3. `06-state-management.md`: five kinds of state and the tool used for each.

Open the files each chapter links as you read: `apps/react-vite/.eslintrc.cjs`, `src/lib/api-client.ts`, and the files in `src/features/discussions/api/`. The guides quote code in a slightly trimmed form (one block replaces lines with `// ...`), so always compare a quoted snippet with the real file before you rely on it. Each chapter ends with **Try it yourself** steps; doing at least one per chapter is the fastest way to be sure of the details the quiz asks about.

excerpts.quote: This is the most important chapter.

readMore.why: The full list of chapters and how they fit together.

notes.title: Concept: organising code by feature
notes.body:
Most tutorials group files by type: all components in one folder, all hooks in another. That stops working once an app has dozens of features, because one change touches five folders and nobody knows what is safe to delete. **Feature-based structure** puts everything one feature needs into one folder, with a thin shared layer under it and an app layer on top.

Read chapter 2, then answer these from the code rather than the prose:

- List the top-level folders in `apps/react-vite/src` and say which of them count as *shared*.
- Open `src/app/routes/app/discussions/discussion.tsx` and note which folders its imports come from.
- In `apps/react-vite/.eslintrc.cjs`, find the `import/no-restricted-paths` rule. For each zone, write in plain words who is restricted and from what. The `target`/`from` naming is easy to read backwards, so check your reading against the chapter's own explanation.
- Note the severity the rule is configured with.

Finally, read the chapter's two footnotes about barrel files and shared `api/` folders.

excerpts.quote: Bulletproof React instead organizes **by feature**, with a thin shared layer underneath and a thin app layer on top.

readMore.why: The lint configuration that enforces the structure.

notes.title: Concept: server data is a cache, not app state
notes.body:
Data fetched from a server is a copy of someone else's state, and it can go stale. A cache library such as TanStack Query (react-query) tracks each copy under a **query key**, refetches it when told it is out of date, and shares it between components that ask for the same key.

Read chapters 5 and 6, then trace the real files:

- `src/lib/api-client.ts`: read both interceptors. For the error handler, go line by line through the 401 branch and write down what each variable holds at runtime.
- `src/features/discussions/api/get-discussions.ts`: note how the query key changes with the `page` argument.
- `src/features/discussions/api/create-discussion.ts`: note which key it invalidates and in what order its `onSuccess` does things. Then look up in the TanStack Query docs how `invalidateQueries` matches keys by default.
- `src/features/discussions/components/discussions-list.tsx`: find where the current page number comes from.

Finally, grep the app for stores created with Zustand and see what they contain.

readMore.why: A mutation declaration with cache invalidation.

notes.title: Single-feature code stays in its feature
notes.body:
In this structure the top-level `components/`, `hooks/` and `utils/` folders mean *shared across features*. A hook that only discussions uses belongs in `features/discussions/` (for example a `hooks/` subfolder created when it is needed). It moves to shared only once a second feature genuinely needs it; premature sharing is how god-folders grow.

- *In src/hooks for later reuse*: the chapter names this as junior mistake number 1.
- *In src/lib*: `lib/` holds preconfigured libraries such as the API client and react-query config.
- *In app/routes*: routes compose features; they are not where feature logic lives.

excerpts.quote: If something is only used by discussions, it does *not* go here

notes.title: The app layer composes features
notes.body:
Rule 1 forbids one feature importing another. The discussion route, `app/routes/app/discussions/discussion.tsx`, imports `DiscussionView` from `@/features/discussions/...` and `Comments` from `@/features/comments/...` and renders them together. The app layer is allowed to import anything, so cross-feature knowledge lives there.

- *Inside features/discussions*: that is a cross-feature import, which the lint zone for discussions rejects.
- *A shared components wrapper*: shared code may not import features at all.
- *Inside features/comments*: the same cross-feature ban applies in the other direction.

notes.title: Reading an import/no-restricted-paths zone
notes.body:
In a zone, `target` is the set of files whose imports are restricted, `from` is the path they may not import, and `except` lists sub-paths of `from` that remain allowed. So this zone says: files in `src/features/auth` may not import from `src/features`, except from `./auth` (their own folder).

- *Other features cannot import auth*: that reverses target and from; other features are limited by their own zones.
- *Only auth routes may import it*: routes are in the app layer, which is not mentioned in this zone.
- *Auth may import every feature except auth*: that reverses the meaning of `except`.

readMore.why: The chapter warning that the zone syntax trips people up.

notes.title: Shared code may not depend on features
notes.body:
The last zone in `.eslintrc.cjs` has `target: ['./src/components', './src/hooks', './src/lib', './src/types', './src/utils']` and `from: ['./src/features', './src/app']`. A file in `src/lib` importing from `src/features/users` matches it, and the rule is configured as `'error'`, so lint fails.

- *Only feature-to-feature imports are banned*: Rule 2 adds the one-way zones, including this one.
- *A warning*: the rule's severity is `'error'` for every zone.
- *Through a barrel*: the restriction is on the path imported from; an `index.ts` inside features is still inside features.

readMore.why: Rule 2: imports flow in one direction.

notes.title: Why barrel files fell out of favour
notes.body:
A barrel file (`index.ts` that re-exports a folder) used to be the suggested public API of a feature. The chapter's footnote says they are no longer recommended because they break Vite's tree-shaking and slow builds. Files are imported by their own path instead, for example `@/features/discussions/api/get-discussions`.

- *Blocked by the lint rule*: `no-restricted-paths` is about which folders may import which, not about barrels.
- *TypeScript cannot resolve @/ through index*: path aliases resolve index files fine; that is not the reason given.
- *Forces one shared api folder*: the shared `api/` folder is a separate, optional alternative discussed in the next footnote.

excerpts.quote: **Barrel files (`index.ts` re-exports) are no longer recommended.**

readMore.why: Direct imports at the top of a real api file.

notes.title: The interceptor returns response.data
notes.body:
`api` is an axios instance whose success interceptor is `(response) => { return response.data; }`. Whatever a caller awaits from `api.get` is therefore already the payload, which is why `getDiscussions` can declare its return type as `Promise<{ data: Discussion[]; meta: Meta }>`.

- *The full axios response*: the interceptor strips the envelope, so `res.data` would be the payload's own `data` field.
- *A react-query result*: react-query wraps the fetcher only when the hook is used; `api.get` itself returns a plain promise.
- *A Zod-parsed object*: no Zod parsing happens on responses in this client.

notes.title: What happens on a 401
notes.body:
The error interceptor first computes `message` and calls `useNotifications.getState().addNotification(...)` for every failed request, so an error toast appears even for a 401. Then, if `error.response?.status === 401`, it sets `window.location.href` to the login path. Finally it returns `Promise.reject(error)`.

- *Retries with a refreshed token*: there is no refresh or retry logic in the client.
- *Silent redirect*: the toast is added before the status check, for every error.
- *Resolves with null*: the handler always rejects.

readMore.why: Centralised error UX and auth handling.

notes.title: An empty URLSearchParams
notes.body:
The 401 branch builds `const searchParams = new URLSearchParams();`, with no argument, so it is empty. `searchParams.get('redirectTo')` is therefore always `null`, and the expression falls back to `window.location.pathname`. The login link always carries just the current path; the page's query string is not kept, and an existing `redirectTo` on the current URL is ignored. The chapter's code block elides these lines with `// ...`, so only the source shows this.

- *The current page's redirectTo*: that would need `new URLSearchParams(window.location.search)`.
- *The full URL with query and hash*: `pathname` holds the path only.
- *The dashboard path*: no default page is used here.

readMore.why: The trimmed snippet in the chapter.

notes.title: invalidateQueries matches by prefix
notes.body:
`getDiscussionsQueryOptions()` with no page gives the key `['discussions']`. TanStack Query's `invalidateQueries({ queryKey })` uses partial matching unless `exact: true` is passed: every cached query whose key starts with the given array is invalidated. `['discussions', { page: 2 }]` starts with `'discussions'`, so it is marked stale and refetched if active.

- *Only the exact entry*: that would require `exact: true`, which the hook does not pass.
- *Only with exact: false*: partial matching is the default; nothing has to be passed.
- *Only on a page change*: invalidation refetches active queries straight away.

readMore.why: The chapter note on reusing the key for invalidation.

notes.title: Shared behaviour first, caller behaviour second
notes.body:
`useCreateDiscussion` destructures `const { onSuccess, ...restConfig } = mutationConfig || {};`. Its own `onSuccess` calls `queryClient.invalidateQueries(...)` and then `onSuccess?.(...args)`. Because the caller's `onSuccess` was pulled out, spreading `restConfig` afterwards cannot replace the shared handler.

- *Instead of the invalidation*: the caller's callback is called from inside the shared one, not in place of it.
- *Before, since restConfig is spread last*: `restConfig` no longer contains `onSuccess`.
- *Never*: it is called with the same arguments right after the invalidation.

notes.title: One small global store
notes.body:
Only `src/components/ui/notifications/notifications-store.ts` imports `create` from `zustand`. It holds the toast queue with `addNotification` and `dismissNotification`. The API client pushes into it from outside React with `useNotifications.getState()`. Once server data, form values and URL state each have their own tool, very little truly global state is left.

- *Fetched discussions*: server data lives in react-query's cache.
- *The current page*: it is URL state, read with `useSearchParams`.
- *Form values*: react-hook-form owns them, validated by the Zod schema.

readMore.why: Application state and the notifications store.

notes.title: The page lives in the address
notes.body:
`discussions-list.tsx` calls `useSearchParams()` and passes `page: +(searchParams.get('page') || 1)` to `useDiscussions`. The page number is part of the URL (`?page=2`), and a refresh reloads the same URL, so the list renders page 2 again.

- *localStorage via react-query*: the query cache here is in memory and is not persisted.
- *The Zustand store*: the only store holds notifications.
- *The router caches component state*: a full reload discards all React state; only the URL survives.

readMore.why: URL state and why it survives a refresh.
